column3: Pairs the placed high anchors with blessing and measured provisions, supporting an integrated life-supporting terrain.
Shows delivered water reviving land, extending the life-giving consequence of the drinking water.
Uses water-service socially, offering only a secondary contrast with environmental provision.
Places livelihoods within the earth, widening the verse's terrain-and-water gifts into provision.

Adds gardens and springs within the earth, closely extending water into cultivated provision.
Defines the earth as a containing system, the immediate ground for its anchored, watered features.
Joins spread earth, anchors, and growth; it supports the same productive-terrain reading while allowing later opening.
Links anchors to preventing sway and to routes, sharpening the stabilizing function alongside access.

Distinguishes sweet, palatable water from salt bitter water while preserving distinct benefits of both.
Contrasts unspoiled and scalding waters in an eschatological setting, secondary to fresh water's goodness.

A fixed meeting time does not add to the terrain or fresh-water reading.
Overflowing water and a vessel provide a contrary scale of water as destructive rather than supplied.

Embodied mercy through birth is only a remote analogue to life-supporting provision.
Memorial function does not clarify mountains or fresh water.
Prepared earth gives a broad habitation parallel, without the verse's anchors or water.
An appointed end for towns only loosely qualifies permanence in the verse's stable arrangement.
Water emerging from the earth under a determined command offers a contrary flood-scale hydrological scene.
Lowly water as reproductive origin is a separate channel from drinkable water and terrain.

Sun exposure and lack of shelter do not clarify the stated mountains or water.
Sleep as a designed interval is only a generic functional parallel.
A secure receptacle for a drop is a secondary containment analogy, not the environmental scene.
A constructed barrier offers a remote analogy to stable separation, not mountains or water.
Mountains becoming like wool provides a contrary limit on any reading of their permanent stability.
Water revives dead land, directly extending its life-giving significance.
Fixed vessels and shared capacity offer only a figurative parallel to stable provision.
Measured safe travel through settled places broadens the idea of a terrain made usable.
Promise and power in this context do not clarify the earth-and-water statement.
Human reproductive allocation is a remote functional parallel only.
A blazing lamp is an upstream environmental condition, but it does not specify the verse's relation.
False speech does not add to the mountain-water reading.
Poured water sustains shade and fruit, extending water into a productive environment.

Differentiated offspring from one source is a remote pattern of ordered formation.

Gushing generative water is a distinct water channel, not fresh water for drinking.

Makes water foundational to living things, broadening the life-giving force of the fresh water.

An elevated truthful reputation does not clarify the environmental statement.
The moral consequence of refusing understanding is unrelated to mountains or water.
Extended dwelling in punishment does not clarify the verse.

The qualities of a distinct drink do not materially clarify fresh terrestrial water.
A plea not to become a trial offers no direct contribution to the verse.
Fixed terms and human families provide only a remote ordered-stage parallel.
Human strength's changing stages only broadly qualify readings of enduring strength.
A garden with rivers ruined by fire offers a contrary image of vulnerable provision.
Latent fire in green trees broadly shows transformed provision, but does not clarify anchors or drinking water.

Names mountains as pegs, directly adding a stabilizing image to the lofty, firm anchors.
Describes water poured down in abundance, extending the supplied drink into its descending source.
Blessed descending water produces gardens and harvest; with 50:7 it closely joins water, growth, and mountains.
Water descends in measure and is lodged in the earth, adding controlled storage to accessible terrestrial water.

Descending provision revives land after death, joining water to the earth's living order.

Gardens and grapevines follow poured water in the same sequence, showing its cultivated outcome.

Stones can yield rivers and springs, offering a direct terrain-to-water connection.

Cloud movement, rain, and hail broaden the atmospheric conditions from which terrestrial water comes.

Mountains provide shade, adding another beneficial function to the raised terrain.
The mountains' being raised directly supports their prominence, though not their water-bearing role.
The mountains' later scattering qualifies their firmness as governed and non-absolute.
Removal of mountains supplies a contrary reading against treating their present stability as permanent.
Mountains that appear fixed yet pass on challenge a purely static account of their stability.
The mountains' movement is a contrary eschatological limit on their ordinary firm placement.
Mountains reduced to dust provide another contrary limit on their durable appearance.
Mountains carried and crushed together show their stability can be ended by a determined event.
Mountains becoming a shifting dune preserve the same contrary, changeable-stability reading.
The removal of mountains adds an eschatological counterpoint to their present emplacement.
The possibility of making drinking water bitter directly qualifies fresh water as a contingent, bestowed condition.
The splitting of earth after water is poured adds the receptive land process behind growth and provision.
Grain brought forth after poured water and split earth makes the water-to-food sequence explicit.
The preceding cultivated outputs are identified as provision for people and livestock, extending the recipient scope.
The visible effects of mercy revive the earth after death, reinforcing the renewal outcome of supplied water.
The earth made as a cradle and traversed by paths supplies the terrain setting immediately before measured water.
After the mountains are dispersed, the land is left level, extending the contrary transformation begun in 20:105.
A mountain sought as refuge against flood gives a contrary scene in which elevated terrain cannot secure against water.
The recession and absorption of floodwater show water's terrestrial distribution can also be withdrawn and bounded.
Rain after scarcity offers a secondary provision-and-renewal parallel.
